# How this software was written — read this first

**The Ada source in this repository was generated by an agentic AI system.**

We are telling you this before you read a line of it, because you would be
entitled to be angry if you found out afterwards.

## What that means, precisely

The pipeline that produced these files is:

1. A **human** read the original C, Fortran or Mortran, chose which component
   was worth converting, and decided **which properties were worth proving**.
   Every target on this list was a human decision.
2. An **agentic AI assistant — Anthropic's Claude, running as a hosted service
   in the United States** — wrote the specification in **prose**. Not Ada: a
   description in English of the types, the operations and the properties to
   state. This is the stage where most of the judgement about *how to say it*
   lives, and it is not a local stage.
3. A **26.9-billion-parameter open-weight model, running locally on a laptop**,
   emitted the Ada/SPARK package specification from that prose. **No human
   hand-wrote the Ada**, and no hosted service saw this step.
4. **GNATprove** — an ordinary, independent, publicly available prover, run
   locally — checked the result against the stated contracts.
5. A **second machine we own**, of different architecture and toolchain,
   re-ran the proof from the source alone and signed a receipt — for eight of the
   eight; `bit_field_packing_pkg` and `carry_forward_rounding_pkg` are proved but not
   yet re-proved and signed. See
   `receipts/`.

So: one human decision, two different AI systems at two different stages, and
two mechanical checks. Steps 4 and 5 are the ones that decide whether anything
here is true, and neither of them is an AI.

## Where the United States enters, stated plainly

We use Anthropic's Claude for step 2, and we are not going to be coy about it in
a repository whose subject is jurisdictional dependence.

What that does and does not mean:

- **The Ada was not written by it.** Step 3 is local and open-weight. The Ada in
  this repository was emitted on a laptop in the north-east of England.
- **The proving is entirely local.** Steps 4 and 5 — the only steps that
  establish anything — run on hardware we own, with a publicly available prover
  and open-source solvers. No hosted service is asked whether a proof holds.
- **Step 2 is replaceable and we know it.** The prose specification is plain
  English. It could be written by a person, or by a local model, at the cost of
  more time and more rounds. Nothing in the method requires a US service; it is
  currently the fastest way for us to do that one stage.
- **You do not have to take that on trust either.** The prose is not secret. If
  it matters to you which system wrote which artefact, ask and we will show you.

We would rather state this than let someone discover it and conclude, fairly,
that a repository arguing about jurisdiction was quiet about its own.

## Why we think this is acceptable, and how to satisfy yourself

**The proof does not depend on trusting the generator.**

An AI writing a proof you must take on faith would be worthless. That is not
what this is. The AI wrote a *claim*; a prover that knows nothing about the AI
then checked it. You can run that prover yourself, on this source, in an empty
directory. If it discharges, the property holds — and it holds regardless of
what wrote the file, or of anything we say about it.

That is the entire reason this work is offered as proofs rather than assurances.

## What HAS been established about this AI-written code

It would be as dishonest to undersell this as to oversell it. Machine-generated
code that nobody checked would be worthless. This is checked, and checked harder
than most hand-written code ever is:

- **The stated properties are proved.** 50 functional contracts discharge. Not
  tested on examples — proved, for every input satisfying the preconditions.
- **Absence of run-time errors is proved.** 76 run-time checks discharge. Within
  the SPARK subset and the stated preconditions, this source is proved free of
  integer overflow, division by zero, range and index violations, and aliasing
  faults — for **all** admissible inputs, not for the ones somebody thought to
  try. In SPARK terms this is AoRTE, and it is the property that ordinarily
  costs the most to obtain.
- **Termination is proved** where it applies: 42 checks.
- **Nothing is justified away.** GNATprove lets you dismiss an unproved check
  with a `pragma Annotate` justification. There are **none** here. 0 justified,
  0 unproved, 0 suppressed.

So the honest summary of the AI's contribution is this: a language model
proposed the text, and everything it proposed has since been machine-checked to
a standard that most software — human-written included — never faces. Where a
property could be proved, it was proved. Where a class of error could be
excluded, it was excluded.

**What remains unproved is stated in the next section, and it is not small.**

## What the AI could still have got wrong, and what proof does not fix

- **The contract may be the wrong contract.** A proof establishes that the code
  satisfies the property *as stated*. If the property is trivial, or does not
  capture what the original actually guarantees, the proof is sound and useless.
  **Read the postconditions and judge them yourself.** This is the real risk
  here, and no amount of proving removes it.
- **The re-expression may not correspond to the original.** These are derived
  works, and the correspondence to the upstream C/Fortran/Mortran is a matter of
  human reading, not proof. We have not proved equivalence with the original,
  and we do not claim it.
- **The prover is not itself proved, and neither is the compiler.** Every claim
  here rests on GNATprove, its back-end solvers, and the GNAT front end being
  correct. None of those is verified software. This is not a rhetorical caveat:
  during this very programme we found a defect that makes gnatprove FSF 15.0
  abort before generating a single proof obligation — a six-line package
  containing an Ada-2022 iterated component association inside an expression
  function. It raises `PROGRAM_ERROR` with no source location on macOS/arm64 and
  a `Storage_Error` stack overflow on Linux/x86-64. Reported upstream as
  AdaCore/spark2014 issue #69.

  Neither that nor anything like it affects the eight cores published here — none
  uses the construct, and all ten discharge cleanly on the released toolchain,
  which you can confirm yourself. But a reader who assumes the trusted base is
  flawless should not.

  We think this is an argument *for* re-running the proof rather than against
  it. If the tool is fallible, the answer is more independent runs on more
  configurations, not fewer.

- **Nothing here is a statement about the upstream software.** No claim is made
  that any original library is unsafe, defective, or deployed anywhere.


## This did not need a frontier model, and that is the point

Every core in this repository was emitted by a **26.9-billion-parameter
open-weight model running locally on a single laptop**. No frontier model, no
API, no cloud, no data leaving the machine. The proving and the independent
re-proving also ran on ordinary hardware we own.

That is not a cost-saving anecdote. It bears directly on why anyone would care
about software sovereignty in the first place:

- **Verification does not require you to send your code to somebody else's
  jurisdiction.** If the argument for checking public-sector software ended with
  "and now upload it all to a hyperscaler", it would defeat itself.
- **The gate does the work, not the model.** A small model proposes; a prover
  disposes. A wrong answer from a 27B model is caught by exactly the same
  mechanism that would catch a wrong answer from the largest model in the world.
  That is what makes the model size a matter of convenience rather than trust.
- **Being unimpressive is a feature.** The honest record: one of these ten took
  four attempts, three of which failed — a use-before-declaration, a bounds
  error the prover caught, and a round that emitted declarations with no bodies
  at all. Every failure was refused. A pipeline whose safety depends on the
  generator being brilliant is a pipeline with no safety; this one assumes the
  generator will be wrong and is built to notice.

So the machine that produced this could sit in a government building in Ottawa
or Québec, air-gapped, owned outright, answering to nobody. **We would rather
that than be the supplier.** The method is the product, and the method is in
this repository.

⚠ We are not claiming a small model is as capable as a large one. It is not. It
needs more rounds and more careful prose. The claim is narrower and more useful:
**with a prover in the loop, it does not have to be.**


## The model that wrote this, named

The generator is **"Rosie"** — our own Ada/SPARK fine-tune of a Qwen model, **26.9B parameters**,
4-bit quantised, run locally under ollama on a laptop. It is not a general-purpose assistant and
is not good at very much; it was trained to emit one kind of artefact.

**The base model, now confirmed:** `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B`. An earlier version of this file said our own
tag and the runtime's architecture string disagreed. They do not disagree — the architecture class
is `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, which belongs to the Qwen3.5 lineage while the model is
Qwen3.8-27B. One model, not two.

⛔ **We previously said we intended to open-source Rosie. We are withdrawing that, and saying so
rather than deleting the sentence.** We have not read the base model's licence — it was never
downloaded with the weights — and we will not distribute a derivative under terms we have not read.

★ **This weakens an argument we made, and we would rather name that than let it pass.** We wrote
that "a small local model is sufficient when a prover checks it" is a claim you should be able to
test, and that you cannot test it against a model you have never seen. That is still true. Not
releasing Rosie does not make the claim false; it makes it **unverifiable from outside**, and you
should weigh it accordingly — as an assertion of ours, not as something you can check.

What matters for judging this repository is unchanged and does not depend on the
model at all: **the proofs discharge, or they do not, and you can run them yourself.**

## Known specifics

- Two checks discharge under only one of the three back-end solvers. Run
  `--prover=z3`, `--prover=cvc5` and `--prover=altergo` separately and you will
  find them.
- The receipts are signed with an interim **software** key, not hardware. The
  right word for them is *measured*, not *attested*.

If your own run disagrees with anything stated here, this repository is wrong
and we would like to know.
